title: Variation of cell potential with concentration: the Nernst equation
objective: To set up the cell Zn | Zn²⁺ ‖ Cu²⁺ | Cu and measure its potential.
To study how the cell potential varies with the concentration of copper sulphate and of zinc sulphate.
To verify the Nernst equation and determine the standard cell potential from a graph.

theory.statement: In a Daniell cell, zinc is oxidised at the anode and copper ions are reduced at the cathode. The difference between the two electrode potentials drives electrons through the external circuit, and the salt bridge completes the circuit inside the cell.
theory.derivationNote: The cell reaction is Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), for which n = 2. The standard cell potential is E° = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. The Nernst equation gives the potential at any concentration as E = E° − (2.303RT/nF)·log Q, where the reaction quotient Q is [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]; the solid metals have unit activity and do not appear. At 298 K the factor 2.303RT/F is 0.0591 V, so E = 1.10 − (0.0591/2)·log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]). A graph of E against log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]) is therefore a straight line of slope −0.0295 V whose intercept is E°. Note that only the ratio matters: if both solutions have the same concentration the logarithm is zero and E equals E° exactly, whatever that common concentration may be.

apparatus.name: Beakers
apparatus.why: Hold the two half-cell solutions separately

apparatus.name: Zinc electrode
apparatus.why: The anode, where oxidation occurs; a clean surface is needed for a steady potential

apparatus.name: Copper electrode
apparatus.why: The cathode, where copper ions are reduced

apparatus.name: Salt bridge
apparatus.spec: U-tube filled with saturated KCl in agar
apparatus.why: Completes the circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral without letting them mix

apparatus.name: Voltmeter
apparatus.why: Measures the e.m.f. while drawing almost no current, so the cell stays at equilibrium

apparatus.name: Volumetric flasks and pipettes
apparatus.why: Prepare the series of accurately diluted solutions

apparatus.name: Thermometer
apparatus.why: The Nernst factor depends on temperature, which must be recorded

materials.name: Copper sulphate solution
materials.why: The cathode electrolyte, varied to test the Nernst equation

materials.name: Zinc sulphate solution
materials.why: The anode electrolyte, varied in the second part of the experiment

materials.name: Potassium chloride
materials.why: Fills the salt bridge; K⁺ and Cl⁻ have almost equal ionic mobilities, so no junction potential is introduced

materials.name: Emery paper
materials.why: Cleans the oxide layer from the metal strips before each run

procedure.text: Clean the zinc and copper strips with emery paper and rinse them with distilled water.
Take 1 M zinc sulphate in one beaker and 1 M copper sulphate in the other. Dip the zinc strip in the zinc sulphate and the copper strip in the copper sulphate.
Connect the two solutions with the salt bridge, making sure both ends are properly immersed.
Connect the zinc electrode to the negative and the copper electrode to the positive terminal of the voltmeter.
Record the steady reading of the voltmeter. This is the standard cell potential, since both concentrations are 1 M.
Replace the copper sulphate with 0.1 M solution, keeping the zinc sulphate at 1 M, and record the new potential.
Repeat with 0.01 M and 0.001 M copper sulphate, recording the potential each time. Note the temperature.
Now keep the copper sulphate at 1 M and vary the zinc sulphate instead, and observe that the potential changes in the opposite sense.
Plot E against log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]). Find the slope and the intercept, and compare them with −0.0295 V and 1.10 V.

steps: For each reading compute the ratio [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] and its logarithm
Plot E on the y-axis against log ratio on the x-axis
Slope = −2.303RT/nF, which is −0.0295 V at 298 K for n = 2
Intercept at log ratio = 0 gives E° of the cell
n may be recovered from the slope as n = −2.303RT/(slope × F)

expectedResult.quantity: Standard cell potential from the intercept

secondary.quantity: Slope of E against log ratio

expectedResult.statement: The cell potential falls by about 0.0295 V for each tenfold increase in the ratio [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺], and the graph of E against the logarithm of that ratio is a straight line of intercept 1.10 V. This confirms the Nernst equation with n = 2.

safety: Copper sulphate is harmful if swallowed and irritates the skin; wash your hands after handling it.
Never pipette any solution by mouth; always use a pipette filler.
Dispose of copper salt solutions in the labelled waste container, not down the sink, as copper ions are toxic to aquatic life.
Handle the emery paper and cut metal strips carefully; the edges are sharp.
Do not short the electrodes directly together, as this discharges the cell and heats the strips.
sourcesOfError: An oxide or tarnish layer on the electrode gives an unsteady and low reading.
A voltmeter of low resistance draws current, so the cell is no longer at equilibrium and reads below the true e.m.f.
A poorly made salt bridge, or one whose ends are not properly immersed, introduces extra resistance and a junction potential.
Concentrations are approximated by activities, which is only accurate for dilute solutions.
Temperature drift changes the Nernst factor during the experiment.
Contamination of one half-cell solution by the other if the salt bridge leaks.

viva.question: What is the function of the salt bridge?
viva.expectedConcept: It completes the electrical circuit by allowing ions to migrate between the two half-cells, and it maintains electrical neutrality in each compartment. Without it, positive charge would build up in the anode compartment and negative charge in the cathode compartment, and the reaction would stop almost immediately.
viva.answerLogic: Both functions: completing the circuit and preserving neutrality.
viva.commonMisconception: Saying it simply lets the two solutions mix.

viva.question: Why is potassium chloride used in the salt bridge rather than some other salt?
viva.expectedConcept: The K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions have almost equal ionic mobilities, so they diffuse at nearly the same rate and no appreciable liquid junction potential develops at either end. The salt must also not react with either electrolyte.
viva.answerLogic: Equal transport numbers minimise the junction potential.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking any soluble salt would do equally well.

viva.question: Write the cell reaction and state the value of n.
viva.expectedConcept: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). Two electrons are transferred, so n = 2.
viva.answerLogic: Balanced redox equation with the electron count.

viva.question: State the Nernst equation for this cell at 298 K.
viva.expectedConcept: E = E° − (0.0591/2)·log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]), with E° = 1.10 V. The solid metals are at unit activity and do not appear in the expression.
viva.answerLogic: Correct Q, correct n, solids omitted.
viva.commonMisconception: Including the concentrations of solid zinc and copper in Q.

viva.question: What happens to the cell potential if the concentration of copper sulphate is decreased?
viva.expectedConcept: The potential falls. Reducing [Cu²⁺] increases the ratio [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺], making the logarithm larger and the subtracted term bigger. This is also what Le Chatelier's principle predicts, since removing a reactant opposes the forward reaction.
viva.answerLogic: Sign of the log term; consistent with Le Chatelier.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting the potential to rise because 'less product' seems favourable.

viva.question: Both solutions are made 0.5 M instead of 1 M. What is the cell potential?
viva.expectedConcept: Exactly 1.10 V, the standard value. The Nernst term depends only on the ratio of the two concentrations, and that ratio is still 1, so its logarithm is zero.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming that any departure from 1 M must change the potential.

viva.question: Why is a high-resistance voltmeter used?
viva.expectedConcept: The e.m.f. is the potential difference when the cell is drawing no current. A low-resistance voltmeter would draw appreciable current, so part of the potential would be lost across the internal resistance and the cell reaction would proceed, changing the concentrations as you measure them.
viva.answerLogic: E.m.f. is defined at zero current.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking any voltmeter measures e.m.f. directly.

viva.question: How is the cell potential related to the Gibbs energy change?
viva.expectedConcept: ΔG = −nFE. A positive cell potential corresponds to a negative Gibbs energy change, that is a spontaneous reaction. For this cell ΔG° = −2 × 96485 × 1.10 ≈ −212 kJ per mole.
viva.answerLogic: Sign relation plus the numerical calculation.
viva.commonMisconception: Omitting the negative sign and concluding that a positive E means non-spontaneous.

viva.question: What would you observe if the electrodes were interchanged, with copper as the anode?
viva.expectedConcept: The calculated standard potential would be −1.10 V, which means the reaction as written is non-spontaneous. In practice the cell would simply operate in the reverse direction: zinc would still be oxidised, and the voltmeter would read on the other side or show a negative value.
viva.answerLogic: A negative E° signals the wrong assignment of electrodes.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing the cell would produce −1.10 V of useful work.

viva.question: Why must the electrodes be cleaned with emery paper before use?
viva.expectedConcept: A layer of oxide or tarnish is a poor conductor and is not the pure metal whose electrode potential is tabulated. It gives an unsteady reading that drifts and is usually lower than the true value.
viva.answerLogic: The measured potential refers to a clean metal surface in contact with its ions.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking cleanliness is only a matter of tidiness.

preLab.question: In the cell Zn | Zn²⁺ ‖ Cu²⁺ | Cu, oxidation occurs at:
preLab.feedback: Zinc has the more negative standard reduction potential, so it is oxidised and acts as the anode.

preLab.question: The standard potential of the Daniell cell at 298 K is:
The value of 2.303RT/F at 298 K is:
preLab.feedback: 2.303RT/F = 0.0591 V at 298 K. Dividing by n = 2 gives the 0.0295 V per decade seen in this cell.

duringLab.question: Record the potential for at least three different concentration ratios.
Keep the salt bridge in place for every reading.
Keep the temperature constant throughout the set of readings.

postLab.question: From the intercept of your graph, state the standard cell potential (V).
postLab.feedback: The intercept at log ratio = 0 gives E° = 1.10 V.

postLab.question: State the slope of your graph of E against log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]) in volts.
postLab.feedback: The slope is −2.303RT/nF = −0.0591/2 = −0.0295 V per decade.

postLab.question: The concentration of Cu²⁺ is reduced from 1 M to 0.01 M while Zn²⁺ stays at 1 M. The cell potential:
postLab.feedback: The ratio increases by two decades, so E falls by 2 × 0.0295 = 0.059 V, from 1.100 to about 1.041 V.

scientificValidation.formula: E = E° − (2.303RT/nF)·log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]); E° = 1.10 V; n = 2; ΔG = −nFE
assumptions: No liquid junction potential at the salt bridge
Electrodes are pure metals of unit activity
Negligible current drawn, so the cell is at equilibrium
scientificValidation.validRange: Concentrations 0.001 to 1.0 mol/L; temperature 288 to 318 K
scientificValidation.unitSystem: Concentration in mol/L, potential in V, temperature in K
edgeCases: Equal concentrations give exactly E°, since log 1 = 0
Salt bridge removed: the voltmeter reads zero — blocked as an error
Identical electrodes give no cell — blocked as an error
Copper as anode gives a negative E° — warned as non-spontaneous
Below 0.001 M the activity assumption fails — warned
expectedBehaviour: A tenfold change in the ratio shifts E by 0.0295 V
Raising [Cu²⁺] increases E; raising [Zn²⁺] decreases it
E against log ratio is linear with r² above 0.995
The number of electrons recovered from the slope is 2
